young.html: Imagine a big group of travelers on horseback: a knight whose tunic is still stained with rust from his armor, a cook, a miller who plays the bagpipes, a nun with her little dogs, a student who loves books more than money, a sailor, a doctor, and a lady from the town of Bath who has been to Jerusalem three times. They are riding together from London to the city of Canterbury, to visit the tomb of a saint. To pass the time, they agree to tell stories.

That is The Canterbury Tales, by Geoffrey Chaucer, written a little over 600 years ago. The innkeeper, Harry Bailly, comes along as judge. Whoever tells the best story will win a free supper at his inn when they get back.

young.html: One of the best-loved tales is told by a priest. It is about a proud rooster named Chauntecleer, who has a bad dream about a fox. His wife, the hen Pertelote, tells him dreams mean nothing. The next morning a sly fox flatters Chauntecleer into closing his eyes and singing, then grabs him by the neck and runs. But the clever rooster talks his way out, and both learn a lesson about flattery.

Your own pilgrimage. With your family, plan a pretend journey. Each person picks a character (a knight, a cook, a student, a sailor ...) and tells a short story that suits that character. Who should be the judge? What prize will the best story win?

For parents: some tales are rude or bawdy. Good ones to share: the Nun's Priest's Tale (the rooster and the fox), the Knight's Tale, the Franklin's Tale, and the Pardoner's Tale (a fable about greed in which three men come to a bad end).

full.html: Geoffrey Chaucer (c. 1343–1400) worked for three kings of England as a soldier, diplomat and official, and wrote poems in his spare hours. He began The Canterbury Tales around 1387 and was still working on it when he died in 1400. He was buried in Westminster Abbey, the first poet in what became Poets' Corner.

The pilgrims are going to the shrine of Saint Thomas Becket in Canterbury Cathedral. Becket, archbishop of Canterbury, was killed in his cathedral in 1170 after a quarrel with King Henry II, and was soon made a saint. His shrine became the most famous pilgrimage site in England.

full.text:
Whan that Aprille with his shoures sote
The droghte of Marche hath perced to the rote, ...
Than longen folk to goon on pilgrimages ...
And specially, from every shires ende
Of Engelond, to Caunterbury they wende,
The holy blisful martir for to seke,
That hem hath holpen, whan that they were seke.
full.work: The Canterbury Tales, General Prologue, lines 1–2 and 12–18
full.author: Geoffrey Chaucer
full.ed: The Complete Works, ed. W. W. Skeat, Clarendon Press
full.note: Glosses: sote, sweet; droghte, dryness; perced to the rote, pierced to the root; longen, long; shires ende, county's end; wende, go; martir, martyr (Becket); seke, to seek, and sick; holpen, helped.

full.html: Read the last two lines aloud: seke ("seek") rhymes with seke ("sick"). Chaucer wrote mostly in rhymed pairs of ten-syllable lines, later called heroic couplets. In his English, a final -e was often sounded: A-pril-le, so-te.

Chaucer, as a pilgrim himself, meets "wel nyne and twenty" travelers at the Tabard Inn in Southwark and describes each one. Together they make a picture of English society: the knightly class (Knight, Squire), the church (Prioress, Monk, Friar, Parson, Pardoner, Summoner), and the working and middle ranks (Merchant, Lawyer, Doctor, Miller, Cook, Shipman, Plowman, the Wife of Bath and more).

full.text:
A Knight ther was, and that a worthy man,
That fro the tyme that he first bigan
To ryden out, he loved chivalrye,
Trouthe and honour, fredom and curteisye. ...
He was a verray parfit gentil knight.
full.work: The Canterbury Tales, General Prologue, lines 43–46 and 72
full.author: Geoffrey Chaucer
full.ed: The Complete Works, ed. W. W. Skeat, Clarendon Press
full.note: Glosses: ryden out, ride out to war; trouthe, faithfulness; fredom, generosity; verray parfit gentil, true, perfect, noble.

full.html: Chaucer's portraits are sly. He seems to praise everyone, but the details tell the truth: the Monk loves hunting more than prayer, the Friar knows every innkeeper better than every poor man, and the Pardoner sells fake relics. A few, such as the poor Parson and his brother the Plowman, are shown as plainly good. The Clerk, a poor Oxford student, is one of them.

full.text:
Souninge in moral vertu was his speche,
And gladly wolde he lerne, and gladly teche.
full.work: The Canterbury Tales, General Prologue, lines 307–308
full.author: Geoffrey Chaucer
full.ed: The Complete Works, ed. W. W. Skeat, Clarendon Press

full.html: The Host proposes that each pilgrim tell two tales on the way and two on the way back; the best wins a supper paid for by the rest. They draw straws, and the Knight goes first. The plan was far too big. Chaucer finished about 24 tales, some of them incomplete, and the pilgrims never get back to the Tabard.

full.title: The Host's plan
full.q: If 30 pilgrims (29 plus Chaucer) each told four tales, how many tales would the book have had? About what fraction did Chaucer write?
full.a: 120 tales; Chaucer wrote about a fifth of the plan

The rooster Chauntecleer, his dream, and the flattering fox.
Three young men set out to kill Death and find a heap of gold instead; their greed destroys them. His theme, in Latin: Radix malorum est cupiditas, "greed is the root of evils."
A wife, a rash promise and a magician; each character tries to outdo the others in generosity.
His jingling "Sir Thopas" is so bad the Host stops him; he tells a long prose tale of wise counsel instead.
A prose sermon on repentance, given as the pilgrims near Canterbury.
full.cap: Some of the tales, summarized in our own words. Others, such as the Miller's and the Reeve's, are rough comedies for adults.

full.html: The links between tales are as lively as the tales. Pilgrims interrupt, quarrel and answer each other. The Miller insists on going next; the Reeve, who was once a carpenter, takes offense; the Wife of Bath gives a long, funny speech about her five marriages and who should rule in a household.

Thinking the book mocks religion. Chaucer satirizes churchmen who betray their calling, which many writers of his time did, but he also gives the Parson, the most admired pilgrim, the last word, and ends the book with a short prayer asking forgiveness for his works.

deep.html: Chaucer did not invent the idea of a frame story: Boccaccio's Decameron has ten young people telling a hundred tales. Chaucer's twist is that his tellers are a mix of every rank, and that the tales reveal the tellers. The story each pilgrim chooses, and the way they tell it, is part of their portrait.

Chaucer wrote in the English of London when French and Latin were still the languages of the court and of learning. The success of his poems helped make London English the basis of written English. William Caxton printed the Tales around 1476, one of the first books printed in England.

The Tales survive in more than 80 manuscripts, in groups called "fragments" whose order is uncertain. Scholars still debate the order Chaucer intended and whether the closing Retraction was meant as an ending.

items: Does a story tell you more about the person who tells it, or about the world?
Chaucer praises good people and mocks hypocrites. Is satire a good way to make people better?
What would a "General Prologue" of your own town or school include?
Why do you think travelers tell stories?

deep.html: Compare Dante's Comedy, another journey with a guide and a goal, and Boccaccio's Decameron. Later on this ladder, Shakespeare inherits Chaucer's English and his gallery of characters.

questions: Which pilgrim would you most like to ride beside? Which would you avoid?
The Host offers a prize for the best story. What makes a story "best": being funny, being true, or teaching something?
In the Nun's Priest's Tale, the fox flatters the rooster and the rooster flatters the fox. How can you tell flattery from real praise?
The Clerk would "gladly lerne, and gladly teche." Who in your life is like that?
Read the first two lines aloud together. What do you hear that sounds like English today?
care: Some tales are bawdy, notably the Miller's, the Reeve's, the Merchant's and the Shipman's. This lesson only names them. The Knight's, Nun's Priest's, Franklin's and Pardoner's tales suit families.
